narrativeReportMd:
# Annotation R4→R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
No hard R4→R6 instance-breaking change was found for local `Annotation` content. The only local material change is a widened `Annotation.author[x]` reference target list: R6 permits `PractitionerRole` as an author reference in addition to the R4 targets.

## Scope
The report analyzes the packaged R4 and R6 `StructureDefinition/Annotation` files and supporting package indexes/metadata. Inherited `Element`/`DataType` hierarchy changes, including the R4 `Element` base versus R6 `DataType` base, are out of scope for this local datatype report.

## Main migration themes
R4 instances that use `authorReference` to Practitioner, Patient, RelatedPerson, or Organization, or `authorString`, remain compatible with the local R6 datatype rules. The migration concern is reverse-direction or mixed-version interoperability: an R6 Annotation may now identify a PractitionerRole as the author, which an R4 target-profile-aware validator or generated model may reject for `Annotation.author[x]`.

## Highest-impact findings
`Annotation:REFERENCE_TARGET:Annotation.author[x]:5e389f` is a medium-impact R6-to-R4 representability risk. It is not a hard R4→R6 validation break because it widens, rather than narrows, the allowed target profile set.

## Findings requiring human review
No finding is flagged as requiring human review. Confidence is high for the computable delta, but lower for the design rationale because official diff and narrative ballot notes were not inspected.

## Backward-compatible design observations
The target-profile addition is probably justified because it allows role-specific attribution without forcing systems to collapse the author to a practitioner, organization, or string. The less disruptive cross-version alternative would be an extension or textual representation, but that would reduce computable interoperability in R6.

## Follow-up analysis
Base `Element`/`DataType` hierarchy changes and the `PractitionerRole` resource's own R4→R6 changes should be handled in their assigned reports.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: No local hard R4→R6 break was found for `Annotation`. The main migration concern is that R6 permits `Annotation.author[x]` to reference `PractitionerRole`, which is not an allowed R4 target and can break R6→R4 validation, round-tripping, or generated-code assumptions. Confidence is high for the StructureDefinition delta and medium for the rationale without official diff/narrative notes.
summary.migrationThemesMd: The local shape of `Annotation` is stable: the same elements are present with the same cardinalities, choice type codes, summary/modifier flags, and local semantic text. Migration work should focus on cross-version handling of author attribution when R6 data uses `PractitionerRole`. Systems that down-convert to R4 need a policy for preserving, textualizing, or extension-carrying that role-specific author information.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high that the only local computable content-model change is the added `PractitionerRole` target profile on `Annotation.author[x]`; this appears in the R6 differential and snapshot and is absent from R4. Confidence in clinical/design rationale is medium because official diffs, ballot notes, and narrative pages were not reviewed. Terminology expansion does not materially affect this assessment because `Annotation` has no local terminology binding.

facts.note: R6 adds PractitionerRole; no R4 target profile was removed.
The choice type codes did not change; only the Reference target-profile domain widened.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element id, path, cardinality, choice codes, summary flag, and definition text are unchanged; the R4 and R6 elements match directly by `Annotation.author[x]`.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is not an R4→R6 validation break because R6 widens the allowed target-profile list. The risk is reverse-direction and runtime interoperability: R6 instances that use `authorReference` to `PractitionerRole/...` are valid against the R6 target list but are outside the R4 target list. Target-profile-aware R4 validators, generated models, and application code that switches over the four R4 author target types may reject or mishandle those instances.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The most likely risk is loss or misinterpretation of author attribution during down-conversion. That can matter for auditability and clinical provenance, but the change does not directly alter the annotation text itself.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow a note's author to be represented as a practitioner acting in a specific role rather than only as a bare Practitioner, Organization, Patient, RelatedPerson, or string.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: the R6 change widens a Reference target list and preserves R4-valid Annotation instances.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal--allowing an annotation author to be a practitioner acting in a specific role--is reasonable, and the computable change is an additive target-profile widening. Because the R4 targets, choice type, cardinality, and element name are preserved, this does not make R4-valid `Annotation.author[x]` instances invalid in R6. The remaining compatibility issue is reverse-version handling when R6 data uses `PractitionerRole`, so the level of R4-to-R6 breakage is effectively none for this local finding. Without official ballot rationale, `Probably justified` is more appropriate than a stronger verdict.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Under the calibration rules, a backward-compatible base-design alternative is not applicable here because the base R6 design is already backward-compatible for R4-to-R6 validation. Keeping the R4 target list unchanged and carrying role-specific authorship in an extension or `authorString` convention could reduce R6-to-R4 validation friction, but that is a down-conversion/profile mitigation rather than a less-breaking R6 base design. It would also make role-specific author attribution less visible to generic R6 validators, serializers, and generated models.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Extension, text, or unchanged-target-list approaches are R6-to-R4 mitigation choices, not needed to avoid R4-to-R6 breakage, and would reduce native computable role attribution in R6.

evidence.detail: R4 target profiles are Practitioner, Patient, RelatedPerson, and Organization.
R6 target profiles add PractitionerRole while preserving the R4 targets.

Package indexes show PractitionerRole exists as a resource StructureDefinition in both R4 and R6; the issue is its absence from the R4 Annotation.author[x] target list, not absence of the resource itself.

examples.examplesMd: The fragment is an `Annotation` datatype value, not a full resource. It illustrates an R6-valid `authorReference` target that a target-profile-aware R4 validator would reject for `Annotation.author[x]`.

findings.narrativeMd: `Annotation.author[x]` is locally widened in R6 by adding `PractitionerRole` to the allowed Reference targets. Existing R4 Annotation instances are not invalidated by this change, but R6 producers can now emit role-specific author references that R4 consumers were not built to accept at this path. The practical consequence is most visible in down-conversion, strict validation, generated SDK target unions, and business logic that assumes an annotation author reference can only be a Practitioner, Patient, RelatedPerson, or Organization.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4-valid Annotation does not become invalid in R6 because no allowed R4 target was removed and no cardinality or type-code constraint was tightened. Conversely, an R6 Annotation with `authorReference.reference = "PractitionerRole/..."` is not cleanly R4-representable under the R4 target-profile list. Strict R4 validators can reject it; looser parsers may accept the JSON shape but lose conformance guarantees or hit downstream type-dispatch errors.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R4→R6 migration, no transform is needed for existing `authorReference` or `authorString` values. For R6→R4 or bidirectional exchange, detect `Annotation.authorReference` values that resolve to `PractitionerRole`. Decide whether to map to the referenced practitioner, map to the organization, convert to `authorString`, or preserve the original reference in an extension/profile-specific rule. Those mappings are potentially lossy because a PractitionerRole can encode role, specialty, organization, and location context that is not represented by a single R4 Annotation author target.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Because the change is an optional widening, it is backward-compatible for R4→R6 validation. The avoidable disruption is specifically for reverse compatibility. A less disruptive cross-version design could have used an extension for role-specific attribution while leaving the target list unchanged, but that would make role attribution less interoperable for native R6 implementations. On balance, the change appears probably justified, with explicit down-conversion guidance needed.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `Annotation.author[x]` keeps the same element name, cardinality, choice shape, and R4 Reference targets, while R6 adds `PractitionerRole` as another allowed Reference target. That means R4-valid Annotation data remains valid under the local R6 datatype rule. The only concrete concern is reverse-direction or mixed-version exchange if an R6 sender uses `authorReference` to a PractitionerRole and an R4 target-profile-aware validator or code path expects only Practitioner, Patient, RelatedPerson, Organization, or string. That is real down-conversion policy work, but it is not a meaningful R4-to-R6 compatibility break for this path.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition-Annotation.json: Annotation.author[x] is 0..1 Reference|string with Reference targets Practitioner, Patient, RelatedPerson, and Organization.
R6 StructureDefinition-Annotation.json: Annotation.author[x] remains 0..1 Reference|string and preserves those targets while adding PractitionerRole.
R4 and R6 package indexes both include StructureDefinition-PractitionerRole; the delta is target-list inclusion on Annotation.author[x], not resource availability.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Annotation is normative in R4, so true R4-to-R6 breaks would need strong justification. Here the normative stability pressure does not change the outcome because this specific path change is additive for R4-to-R6 validation and leaves existing R4 author representations intact.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: an R6 Annotation can now use authorReference=PractitionerRole/..., which is outside the R4 Annotation.author[x] target list; there is no old-valid/new-invalid R4-to-R6 instance break.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: No less-breaking base R6 design is needed for R4-to-R6 compatibility because the base change is already a widening. Leaving PractitionerRole out and relying on authorString or an extension would reduce reverse-version friction, but it would also make role-specific author attribution less computable and less visible to generic R6 tooling.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing impact and alternative judgment: agree that there is no hard R4-to-R6 break and no useful less-breaking base design, but the medium-impact framing overstates this finding under the fresh R4-to-R6 review rubric because the compatibility issue is reverse-direction only.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: The canonical URL, id, name, kind, type, status, abstract flag, and specialization derivation are stable. The baseDefinition changed from `Element` to `DataType`, but that is an inherited/base hierarchy issue and excluded from local findings.

Both snapshots contain the same local/inherited element paths: `Annotation`, `Annotation.id`, `Annotation.extension`, `Annotation.author[x]`, `Annotation.time`, and `Annotation.text`. The Annotation differential contains the same four local element ids in both versions.
Local cardinalities are unchanged: root `0..*`, `author[x]` `0..1`, `time` `0..1`, and `text` `1..1`.

The local choice/primitive type codes are unchanged: `author[x]` remains `Reference|string`, `time` remains `dateTime`, and `text` remains `markdown`. The Reference target-profile widening on `author[x]` is reported separately as a material finding.
`Annotation` has no local terminology bindings in either R4 or R6, so terminology expansion comparison is not applicable.

No local Annotation-specific constraints were added, removed, or changed in the differential. Snapshot constraint differences are inherited from base Element/Extension definitions and are out of scope for this report.
No fixed values, patterns, or default values are present on local Annotation elements in either version.
No local minValue, maxValue, maxLength, or regex constraints were found on Annotation elements in either version.
The root and local elements are not modifiers in both versions.
The summary flags on local elements are unchanged: `author[x]`, `time`, and `text` are summary elements; inherited `id` and `extension` are not.
No slicing is present on local Annotation elements in either version.
The local short, definition, comment, mappings, and summary flags for `Annotation`, `author[x]`, `time`, and `text` are materially unchanged.
No element was renamed or moved. JSON/XML property names for the local datatype remain stable (`authorReference`/`authorString`, `time`, `text`).

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: PractitionerRole added as an author Reference target
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The change widens the allowed target-profile set. R4 data that used an allowed R4 target remains valid against this aspect of the R6 definition.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: The widened target is still important for mixed-version ecosystems because R6 data using `PractitionerRole` cannot be validated as an R4 Annotation without transformation or a profile/extension policy.
